title: Eddie Chance calls: jazz is only 55 years old and came out of Chicago
summary: Eddie Chance, Tom Brown's nephew, argues about where jazz was named, praises Emmett Hardy and Red Bolman and says real jazz comes from the body.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels

blocks.x: baby. That will be coming up shortly, but we want to go back to the multi-phones with another call here for you. Good morning. You're on the air with Dick Allen of Tulane University. And Mr. Johnny Wiggs. Yes, sir. Go ahead. This is Eddie Jazz. One of the original jazz man. See, I like to set the record straight about jazz. Jazz is only 55 years old. There's no such thing as jazz before that. And that was just what's going on now. Everybody is using one another's questions about jazz. Now, I'm related to Tom Brown, and I also played with Johnny Wiggs. I hope Johnny Wiggs don't misunderstand this conversation. But I think that I played with the greatest. I played with Stoji Quinn. And Rat Report. Well, I'll say the greatest. In fact, I had them in my band. And jazz, when they come on and say that jazz is originated here and there and other places, no. Uh-uh. It haven't been resonated nowhere but in Chicago. And the reason why it was originated at Chicago, because they couldn't play that style of music, and when they couldn't play it, then they called it jazz to hoit the band. But there was never a band called jazz, even to colored bands. Colored bands never did use the name of jazz. Ragtime, but not jazz. And I think that I'm knowing enough, and I believe I know enough people up in the age can back up what I'm saying, that jazz is a big word. If you don't have it, you can't play it. And if you read it, then you're not playing jazz. And if they got people that trying to work themselves in on the credit of something, you notice today, since New Orleans Jazz Club started, they went ahead, and everybody come along is a jazz musician. But if they ever did play a jazz number, they could be happy for the separate reason that you take men like Harry Shields and Raymond Boyk. They're about the best right now because the other ones is deceased. But Rat Reporter was a great client at band. Now, on Trumpet, you talked about this boy lived across the river that...

Johnny said that nobody hurt him. I can't think of his name right now. But he played against Louis Armstrong on a boat, and Louis Armstrong put his horn down, said that he could pass Emmett Hardy that I'm talking about.
Yeah, the man who never recorded, Eddie.

He never did record, no, because he didn't have the chance. But there were so many great trumpet players, like Red Borman, that was another great trumpet man. And it takes quite a few. In fact, I mean, we have still some fine jazz men, but they just don't get together. And when they don't get together, what they do, they organize the band, and they'll organize to their satisfaction. They get a drum player that don't know the beats, and then they call themselves. If you're going to have a jazz band, every man in that band has got to play jazz. And if one man is not playing jazz, he automatically corrupts the other man, because the man that plays jazz plays from the body. He cannot play. You take myself. I made a few records, and I tried to play with my records. And I cannot, because I can't duplicate what I've done that time. I can't duplicate the same beats that I made. And there's no jazz musician can play the same number twice the same. That's why I never could write it.
